questions.question: Q1. What is the central planning question this experiment addresses before a scanning session even begins?

answers.a: Which colour scheme to use when displaying the point cloud on screen
answers.b: How finely to sample the surface based on feature size, distance, and time constraints
answers.c: Which file format to save the final point cloud in
answers.d: Whether to use a tripod or handheld scanning method

explanations.a: Not quite! Colour display is just a visualisation choice. We're focusing on the physical geometry of capturing the data.
explanations.b: Spot on! Before you even start scanning, you have to decide how finely to sample. Go too coarse, you miss details; go too fine, you waste time and storage.
explanations.c: Not quite! File formats are a data storage concern addressed after the scan is done.
explanations.d: Not quite! Tripods vs. handhelds are logistical choices, separate from the math of resolution.

questions.question: Q2. According to the point spacing formula Δs = Z / fx, what happens to point spacing if the scanning distance Z is doubled while the focal length fx stays constant?

answers.a: Point spacing is halved, making the scan denser
answers.b: Point spacing doubles, making the scan sparser
answers.c: Point spacing stays exactly the same regardless of distance

explanations.a: Not quite! Since Z is in the numerator, increasing it increases point spacing.
explanations.b: Spot on! Doubling the distance (Z) directly doubles the point spacing, making the scan sparser. The further away you are, the more spread out the points get.
explanations.c: Not quite! Point spacing explicitly depends on distance—that's why Z is in the formula!
explanations.d: Not quite! Doubling a positive number while dividing by another positive constant won't ever give you zero.

questions.question: Q3. What is the practical rule of thumb for reliably detecting a feature in a point cloud?

answers.a: The feature size should be exactly equal to the point spacing
answers.b: The feature size should be at least 2 to 3 times larger than the point spacing
answers.c: The feature size is irrelevant; any feature can be detected
answers.d: The feature size should be smaller than the point spacing

explanations.a: Not quite! If they're equal, the feature might fall right between two points and vanish entirely.
explanations.b: Spot on! Just like the Nyquist theorem, you need enough points landing on a feature to actually see it. Making sure the feature is 2 to 3 times larger than your spacing gives you a solid safety net.
explanations.c: Not quite! If a feature is too small for the spacing, it slips through the gaps in the grid.
explanations.d: You've got it backward! If a feature is smaller than the point spacing, it's almost guaranteed to be missed.

questions.question: Q4. If a task requires detecting a minimum feature size of 4mm, and you use a safety margin of m=4, what is the maximum permissible point spacing (Δs_max)?

explanations.a: Not quite! Looks like you multiplied 4 by 4 instead of dividing.
explanations.b: Not quite! That's just the feature size itself, which gives you zero safety margin.
explanations.c: Spot on! 4mm divided by 4 gives a maximum spacing of 1mm. This guarantees your points are tight enough to capture the feature safely.
explanations.d: Not quite! You divided by 16 (4 squared) instead of simply dividing by 4.

questions.question: Q5. Using Δs_max of 1mm from Q4 and a sensor with focal length fx = 700 px, what is the maximum usable scanning distance Z_max?

explanations.a: Not quite! Looks like you divided instead of multiplying.
explanations.b: Spot on! 1mm × 700 gives you 700mm. If you move further back than this, your point spacing will be too wide to reliably catch the 4mm feature.
explanations.c: Not quite! 1 multiplied by 700 is 700, not 70.
explanations.d: Not quite! You added an extra zero there!

questions.question: Q6. What happens to the number of pulses required per rotation (N) for a LiDAR sensor if the angular resolution is made twice as fine?

answers.a: N is halved, requiring fewer pulses
answers.b: N doubles, requiring twice as many pulses

explanations.a: You've got it backward! Making the resolution finer means the angle gets smaller, which requires more pulses.
explanations.b: Spot on! If you cut the angular step in half, you need twice as many pulses to complete a 360-degree sweep. This directly doubles your scan time or requires the laser to fire twice as fast.
explanations.c: Not quite! N is directly linked to angular resolution; change one, and the other must change.
explanations.d: Not quite! A pulse count can't be negative in the real world.

questions.question: Q7. For an image-based sensor, what happens to processing time and storage size if you double the resolution in both width and height?

explanations.a: Not quite! More pixels directly equal more data to store and process.
explanations.b: That's an underestimation! You're doubling two dimensions at once.
explanations.c: Spot on! Doubling both the width and height means 2 × 2 = 4 times the pixels. That translates to four times the data and processing time. Quality comes at a cost!
explanations.d: Not quite! More resolution means more pixels, not fewer.

questions.question: Q8. Why can't a single scan configuration simultaneously maximise high resolution, short scan time, AND full object coverage?

answers.a: Hardware manufacturers deliberately limit their sensors
answers.b: These are competing physical constraints—more detail over a large area takes more time or wildly expensive hardware
answers.c: Actually, modern scanners can achieve all three easily
answers.d: This limit only applies to LiDAR, not stereo cameras

explanations.a: That's a myth! It's a fundamental physics limit, not a manufacturer conspiracy.
explanations.b: Spot on! This is the classic resolution-time-detail triangle. Capturing more spatial detail over a wider area inherently takes more measurements. You have to sacrifice one to get the other two.
explanations.c: Actually, that goes against physics. Better tech shifts the boundaries, but the fundamental trade-off always remains.
explanations.d: Not quite! The physics of sampling applies universally across all 3D scanning technologies.

questions.question: Q9. What is voxel grid downsampling, and why would you use it?

answers.a: A technique to artificially increase resolution beyond what was scanned
answers.b: A method to reduce an over-sampled point cloud by keeping one point per grid cell
answers.c: A method for adding colour to a point cloud
answers.d: A way to merge two separate point clouds

explanations.a: Not quite! Downsampling reduces resolution; you can't magically create data the sensor didn't capture.
explanations.b: Spot on! It's the inverse of planning a scan: if you captured way too much detail, voxel downsampling groups points into cubes and keeps one per cube, shedding unnecessary weight for faster processing later.
explanations.c: Not quite! This is purely about geometry and point density, not colour.
explanations.d: Not quite! Merging scans is called registration (like ICP). Downsampling is for thinning out a single scan.

questions.question: Q10. Why do scanning a bridge for structural shifts and scanning a machined part for sub-millimetre flaws require completely different resolution planning?

answers.a: They don't; standard settings work for both
answers.b: The minimum feature sizes differ enormously, requiring different point spacing and distances
answers.c: The difference is only due to the colour of the materials
answers.d: Bridge scanning always requires higher resolution

explanations.a: Actually, that goes against the entire point of the experiment! One-size-fits-all settings waste time or miss crucial data.
explanations.b: Spot on! A bridge involves massive, centimetre-scale features, allowing for coarse spacing and long-distance scanning. The machined part requires capturing tiny flaws, demanding ultra-fine spacing up close. The math is the same, but the goals dictate vastly different setups.
explanations.c: Not quite! Geometric resolution is completely unrelated to object colour.
explanations.d: Not quite! It's actually the reverse. Finding a tiny flaw in a machined part requires much higher point density than looking for a slight bend in a massive bridge.
